news.title: Robot tasks get a difficulty ladder tested through learning
news.summary: A National University of Singapore team and partners proposed 112 simulated robot tasks. Four levels are assigned by observing how the same model learns from the same number of examples.
news.details: A team including the National University of Singapore posted ManiLadder on November 12, a study introducing 112 simulated object-manipulation tasks organized into four difficulty levels. The collection covers rigid and deformable objects, one or two arms, simple grippers and multi-finger hands. The researchers want to measure not only the variety of actions a robot learns but also how demanding a task it can solve under a common learning budget.
news.technical_novelty: A National University of Singapore team and partners proposed 112 simulated robot tasks. Four levels are assigned by observing how the same model learns from the same number of examples. Calibration gives each task 20 demonstrations and the same reference control model with fixed training settings. The model learns to reproduce demonstrated actions, and its success determines the task's level. It trains for 40,000 steps, with 50 evaluation attempts every 5,000 steps. Task conditions are revised until performance falls within the intended range. Final method comparisons also use 50 test attempts per task, with evaluation starting conditions separated from those used to collect demonstrations.
news.engineering_impact: A National University of Singapore team and partners proposed 112 simulated robot tasks. Four levels are assigned by observing how the same model learns from the same number of examples. The idea resembles selecting tasks for progressively developing a skill, but here difficulty comes from experiments with a learning program. Changing a mug's starting position or a box's size can require a different movement sequence. The authors vary such conditions and observe the reference program's success. This organizes comparison around the demands of the actions rather than a long list of task names. Further tests with other models examine how much of the ordering survives beyond the original calibration setup.
news.limitations: A National University of Singapore team and partners proposed 112 simulated robot tasks. Four levels are assigned by observing how the same model learns from the same number of examples. The scale has a specific anchor: a reference model and twenty examples per task. More data or a different learning method can change where a task sits on that scale. Training conditions therefore remain part of the comparison, alongside the displayed success rate.
news.evidence_status: An author-published research paper and evaluation protocol; the reported results were obtained by the research team.
news.organization: National University of Singapore and collaborating universities

news.title: A robot hand benefits when its fingers describe force in the same frame
news.summary: A University of York team and partners built a hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Finger signals are transformed into shared coordinates so the program can compare force directions consistently.
news.details: Researchers at the University of York, with colleagues in Edinburgh, Jena and King's College London, posted a paper on November 11 about DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand for detaching adhered objects, cleaning surfaces and retrieving obscured targets. Each fingertip measures force along three axes. To compare readings as the fingers bend, the authors transform them into a shared coordinate frame attached to the wrist. Each force direction is then described relative to the same reference rather than a differently oriented finger.
news.technical_novelty: A University of York team and partners built a hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Finger signals are transformed into shared coordinates so the program can compare force directions consistently. Each control program learns from 20 successful demonstrations collected through human operation. It receives three camera views, joint states and selected fingertip observations. Across six core tasks, mean success rose from 24% with cameras and joint information alone to 83% when fingertip position and orientation, along with forces expressed in wrist coordinates, were added. That comparison changes several inputs together; intermediate configurations help examine their contributions. Three further scenarios were evaluated with the full configuration. The paper has been accepted by IEEE Transactions on Robotics, a research journal.
news.engineering_impact: A University of York team and partners built a hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Finger signals are transformed into shared coordinates so the program can compare force directions consistently. Imagine an arrow drawn on a glove: turning your hand also turns the arrow relative to the table. A sensor attached to a finger creates a similar description problem. Researchers use joint geometry to express forces relative to one wrist reference. The physical contact stays the same; the representation supplied to the program changes. It illustrates how useful sensor data depend on both the measurement and the coordinate system that gives its components meaning, especially when several fingers move independently.
news.limitations: A University of York team and partners built a hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Finger signals are transformed into shared coordinates so the program can compare force directions consistently. The experiments cover a place where the hand has already been positioned: the wrist remains fixed and a stage raises or lowers it. Searching a large room and positioning an entire robotic arm are outside this experimental setup and are identified by the authors as further integration work.
news.evidence_status: Author-run experiments; accepted by IEEE Transactions on Robotics. Input comparisons cover six core tasks; independent reproduction is not established here.
news.organization: University of York; University of Edinburgh; Friedrich Schiller University Jena; King’s College London

news.title: Japan discusses what will help robots reach working sites
news.summary: Japan's government met robot and component makers. Alongside machines and software, companies requested support for data and several years of early adoption.
news.details: Japan's prime minister Sanae Takaichi met robot and component makers on November 12 to discuss support for physical AI, artificial-intelligence systems that guide actions in the physical world. She instructed ministers to reflect company requests in the growth-strategy implementation plan and provide predictable information about support measures and required budgets. The meeting reiterated 2040 ambitions: deploying roughly 10 million AI robots and securing a global market share for Japanese industry of more than 30%, or 20 trillion yen.
news.technical_novelty: Japan's government met robot and component makers. Alongside machines and software, companies requested support for data and several years of early adoption. Companies identified four needs: support from domestic robot and component research through volume production; faster development of domestic AI technologies; mechanisms for accumulating data; and multi-year support for early adoption. The government links robotics to worker shortages, physical workload and hazardous operations. The published speech assigns these issues to further planning, with specific support amounts still to be set out. A separate Sankei report published by ITmedia on November 13 corroborates the meeting and the targets.
news.engineering_impact: Japan's government met robot and component makers. Alongside machines and software, companies requested support for data and several years of early adoption. Behind a robot demonstration lies a chain of work: making components, teaching control, finding a suitable site and checking operation alongside people. The meeting considered those parts together. The industry story therefore concerns conditions under which different developers can offer systems to customers. The market target signals policy direction, while the request for multi-year support explains why participants need planning beyond a short demonstration. The government assigned the question of predictable support to the responsible minister as part of the implementation plan.
news.limitations: Japan's government met robot and component makers. Alongside machines and software, companies requested support for data and several years of early adoption. The published speech identifies the next step: put company requests into the growth-strategy plan and specify support measures with required budgets. Market participants will then be able to examine the programs on which they could rely when organizing actual deployments.
news.evidence_status: Official policy speech corroborated by Sankei reporting; targets and instructions are presented as government plans.

The meeting reiterated 2040 ambitions: deploying roughly 10 million AI robots and securing a global market share for Japanese industry of more than 30%, or 20 trillion yen.

news.title: Outside applications can request trips from Serve's sidewalk robots
news.summary: Serve Robotics opened software access to its delivery service. Developers can first test requests with simulated robots and then seek permission to use the physical network.
news.details: U.S. company Serve Robotics opened a developer portal for its sidewalk delivery-robot network on November 11. An application can request a delivery, specify collection and drop-off, and track the trip through an application programming interface, or API: a set of commands for communicating with the service. Serve also provides a test environment containing simulated robots. Documentation and this environment are available immediately; live-robot access requires company approval and service coverage at the requested location.
news.technical_novelty: Serve Robotics opened software access to its delivery service. Developers can first test requests with simulated robots and then seek permission to use the physical network. Serve reports a network of 2,000 robots across more than 150 neighborhoods in 20 U.S. cities. Dispatch, routes, navigation and operational supervision remain with the operator. Developers build services on top of that infrastructure, such as delivery for a local shop. The simulated environment allows them to test the full delivery sequence and unusual situations before using a physical machine. The network figures are company-reported, and the allocation of operating responsibilities also comes from Serve’s description.
news.engineering_impact: Serve Robotics opened software access to its delivery service. Developers can first test requests with simulated robots and then seek permission to use the physical network. A new participant can focus on a shop or ordering application rather than developing a wheeled machine. It specifies collection and handover using commands the service understands, while Serve remains responsible for routing and supervision. Robotics becomes one part of a broader service: the customer wants a purchase to arrive, and the application must coordinate shop, operator and recipient. The simulated environment allows this sequence to be checked without a street trip, including unusual situations that a team wants to investigate before physical delivery.
news.limitations: Serve Robotics opened software access to its delivery service. Developers can first test requests with simulated robots and then seek permission to use the physical network. The next boundary is the service map and operator approval. Developers need actual collection and handover points within the supported network. Planning a useful integration therefore includes the physical geography of the trip as well as communication between pieces of software.
news.evidence_status: Official Serve release and technical explanation; network size and available functions are operator-reported.

news.title: Five hundred million dollars backs industrial robotics expansion
news.summary: Agile Robots raised new capital in a SoftBank Group-led round. The company, valued at $8.5 billion, combines arms, hands, mobile robots and humanoids.
news.details: Agile Robots raised $500 million in a Series F financing round at an $8.5 billion valuation, reported by Reuters and Forbes on November 12. A financing round is a further stage of raising capital from investors. SoftBank Group led it, with NVIDIA, Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures, and T.Capital among the participants. Total capital raised reached $2 billion. The company links the new money to U.S. expansion, greater production capacity including in Germany, and entry into new markets.
news.technical_novelty: Agile Robots raised new capital in a SoftBank Group-led round. The company, valued at $8.5 billion, combines arms, hands, mobile robots and humanoids. Agile Robots offers industrial arms, robotic hands, mobile systems and humanoids. It reports more than 20,000 industrial robotic solutions installed with customers. Its Fürstenfeldbruck site near Munich has stated capacity for up to 10,000 legged or wheeled humanoid robots a year. These figures describe different parts of the business: installed industrial equipment and capacity to produce new machines. Forbes connects investor interest with the combination of manufacturing, software and established industrial-automation experience.
news.engineering_impact: Agile Robots raised new capital in a SoftBank Group-led round. The company, valued at $8.5 billion, combines arms, hands, mobile robots and humanoids. The investment shows which capabilities market participants are backing. Here the company connects device development with integration into industrial work. Acquired businesses such as Franka Robotics contribute different parts of that offer. Robot adoption also involves fitting equipment into a customer's operation and supporting it afterward. Money for manufacturing sites and international expansion therefore affects where customers may obtain hardware and assistance, in addition to the design of an individual robot. That industrial network is part of the investment story described by the company and Forbes.
news.limitations: Agile Robots raised new capital in a SoftBank Group-led round. The company, valued at $8.5 billion, combines arms, hands, mobile robots and humanoids. The official announcement names the United States and capacity expansion including Germany. It does not disclose utilization of new lines or individual order terms, leaving subsequent production information as the basis for assessing how quickly that planned capacity is being used.
news.evidence_status: Company financing announcement checked against Forbes and Reuters; production capacity and installed base are company-reported.
